name: Santander
title: Santander Ship UTM | Ferry and Vehicle Carrier Gauging
description: Ultrasonic thickness gauging at Santander for ro-pax ferries, car carriers, bulkers and tankers: ballast tanks, vehicle decks, ramps and pre-docking readings.
h1: Thickness Gauging for Ferries and Cargo Ships in the Bay of Santander
intro: Santander is a wide, sheltered bay on the Cantabrian coast with a ferry terminal for services to England, busy car and ro-ro quays, and bulk and project berths on the southern shore. Ships here work to timetables and carry heavy vehicle loads. Technicians travel from India to the ship for ultrasonic gauging, planned around turnarounds and lay-overs, and fed into survey preparation or a docking at a yard on the bay or the coast.

highlights.p: Ro-pax ships on the English Channel crossings turn around on tight schedules. Readings on ballast tanks, vehicle decks and ramp structure are fitted into the lay-over so the sailing is not delayed.
Car decks wear under wheel loads and wash-down water, and ramps flex with every call. We gauge deck plating, ramp hinges and framing and report where the steel has thinned.

highlights.h: A large bay with several working areas
highlights.p: Santander's bay holds ferry berths, vehicle quays, bulk terminals and a repair yard. We plan each job against the berth the ship is actually using, not the port in general.

port.h: The Bay of Santander: ferries, vehicles and bulk on the Cantabrian coast
p: The bay is a large natural inlet on the north coast of Spain, entered past a headland and a long sandy spit, and the port authority, the Autoridad Portuaria de Santander, has quays on several sides of it. The central quays near the city take cruise ships and the ferry terminal, while Raos, Maliaño and the southern shore take industrial cargoes. Once inside the entrance the water is calm, though a strong north-westerly can make the approach lively and occasionally holds ships at sea until the swell eases.

Passenger services give Santander a distinct place among Spanish ports: Brittany Ferries operates ro-pax ships on crossings between Santander and the south coast of England, and those vessels lie in port for a few hours between sailings. Beside them, the port is a major handler of cars and other vehicles, with ro-ro and car-carrier ships working the quays all week. Bulk cargoes include cement, fertiliser, grain and industrial minerals, and liquid bulk and general cargo ships call for the industries around the bay. A repair yard on the bay serves smaller commercial vessels.

Inspection demand follows that pattern. Ferry owners carry out regular structural checks because the ships run year-round across the Bay of Biscay and the Channel approaches, and the vehicle decks, ramps and stabiliser-related structure see heavy cyclic loading. Car carriers have very large, light-framed hulls with high windage, and their side shell, ramps and deck plating are common gauging subjects. Bulk and cargo ships bring the more familiar needs: hold frames, tank tops, ballast tanks and deck plating ahead of a survey or a sale.

facilities.h: Where gauging happens around the bay
p: Most readings are taken alongside. Ferries in the passenger terminal are gauged during their turnaround or an extended lay-over, usually in the ballast tanks, on the vehicle decks and in the spaces near ramps and stern doors. Car carriers at the vehicle quays are measured between loading and discharge, when decks are clear and ramps can be lowered for access. Bulk carriers and general cargo ships at the southern-shore terminals allow hold and tank access once cargo is out, and gauging in the machinery spaces covers sea water piping and scrubber lines on ships that have them.

Drydock work is available in the bay itself, where a shipyard serves coasters, tugs, workboats and some larger merchant ships, and further along the northern coast where bigger yards deal with larger vessels. An owner can therefore gauge at Santander, send the steel list to the yard of choice and have technicians return in dock for post-blast readings. Roads outside the bay can be used for pre-arrival gauging by launch, but in practice most ships are gauged alongside because the bay offers sheltered berths.
list: Passenger and ferry berths: ballast tanks, vehicle decks, ramps and stern door structure gauged between sailings
Vehicle and ro-ro quays: car carrier side shell, deck plating and ramp hinges between cargo operations
Bulk terminals on the southern shore: hold frames, tank tops and hopper tanks on bulkers carrying cement, grain and minerals
General cargo and project quays: deck, hatch cover and tank structure on conventional cargo ships
The bay's repair yard and slipways: smaller ships hauled out or docked for repair
Anchorage inside the bay: pre-docking gauging by launch for ships waiting for a berth or a yard slot

context.h: Regulation, ferry operations and EU rules in Santander
p: Port state control at Santander is carried out for the Paris MoU by inspectors of the Capitanía Marítima under the Dirección General de la Marina Mercante. Ro-pax ships fall under the EU's harmonised survey requirements for passenger ships, and their owners maintain structural records closely; thickness readings on ballast tanks and vehicle decks are a regular part of that evidence, particularly when a ship nears a special survey or a sale. Cargo ships on short-sea routes through the bay are inspected on the usual risk basis.

EU measures now shape ferry and short-sea economics as well. EU ETS applies to voyages between EU ports and to part of those between EU and non-EU ports, which includes crossings to England in part, and FuelEU Maritime sets intensity limits on the energy used. Operators therefore look hard at hull condition, propulsion efficiency and retrofit options, and structural gauging precedes any retrofit that opens the hull. The Ship Recycling Regulation also requires an Inventory of Hazardous Materials on ships calling at EU ports, which owners of older ro-ro tonnage deal with alongside survey planning.

jobs.p: Santander requests mix scheduled ferry work with cargo-ship surveys. Ferry operators plan programmes months ahead, so travel and visas can be fixed early; cargo ships bring shorter notice and a narrower scope. Each job is planned with the superintendent, and magnetic particle equipment accompanies the team when ramps, hinges or frame ends are on the list. Examples include:
list: Ballast tank and double-bottom gauging on a ro-pax ferry during a long lay-over, supporting the structural record before its special survey.
Vehicle deck plating readings on a car carrier at the vehicle quays, with magnetic particle testing at ramp hinges and framing connections.
Stern door, side door and ramp structure gauging on a ferry whose owner wants quantified wear on hinges and seals mountings.
Hold frame and tank top gauging on a bulk carrier discharging cement or minerals, measured against the diminution limits for its survey.
Pre-docking readings on a coaster lying in the bay, producing a steel estimate for the yard before the ship is hauled out.

logistics: Technicians fly from India to Madrid or another European hub and then to Santander Airport, or arrive through Bilbao and travel by road along the coast. Port and terminal access is requested by the ship's agent, who also arranges launches for any anchorage work. Spanish entry for Indian nationals requires a Schengen visa, so the team plans around visa issue and the ship's schedule; ferry work is easiest because sailing dates are known well in advance.

faqs.q: Can a ferry be gauged during a normal turnaround at Santander?
faqs.a: A turnaround of a few hours allows a limited programme, mainly accessible ballast tanks and parts of the vehicle decks. A longer lay-over or a scheduled maintenance stop allows a full set of readings. We agree the priority list with the technical superintendent and tell you honestly what can be done without affecting the ship's sailing.

faqs.q: What is measured on a car carrier?
faqs.a: Deck plating, ramp structure and hinges, side shell near ramp openings and the framing under decks that carry heavy vehicles. Wash-down water and cyclic loading cause wastage that is not always obvious from inside the ship. We add magnetic particle testing at connections where cracking is suspected and report readings by deck and frame position.

faqs.q: Is there a drydock in the Bay of Santander?
faqs.a: There is a repair yard in the bay that handles smaller commercial ships, tugs and workboats. Larger merchant ships and ferries usually dock at bigger yards elsewhere on the northern coast. Gauging at Santander before the docking gives the yard a steel list in advance and shortens the time the ship spends out of service.

faqs.q: Do Atlantic swells interfere with gauging inside the bay?
faqs.a: Inside the bay the quays are calm, so alongside work proceeds normally. Swells mostly affect the approach and timing of arrival. We keep technician travel flexible, because a ship delayed outside the bay can reach the berth later than planned, and the schedule is updated with the agent as the ship's position becomes clear.

faqs.q: Can you gauge scrubber piping on ships calling at Santander?
faqs.a: Yes, where the ship has an exhaust gas cleaning system and the scrubber space is accessible. We measure wash-water, overboard and discharge piping and adjacent plating, since corrosive wash-water wears these lines fast. Readings are reported by pipe run and plate so the owner can plan replacements for a convenient stop.
